THEORY — Signs in the four quadrants (ASTC rule):
  • 1st quadrant (0–90°): all ratios positive — All
  • 2nd (90–180°): only sin and cosec positive — Silver
  • 3rd (180–270°): only tan and cot positive — Tea
  • 4th (270–360°): only cos and sec positive — Cups

The derivative dy/dx measures the rate of change of y with respect to x — geometrically, the slope of the curve at that point. The master rule is d/dx (xn) = n·xn−1: “the power comes down in front, and the power decreases by one.”

entries.name: THEORY — The three working rules
entries.body:
THEORY — The three working rules:
  • Product rule: d/dx (u·v) = u·(dv/dx) + v·(du/dx) — “first × derivative of second + second × derivative of first.”
  • Quotient rule: d/dx (u/v) = v(du/dx) − u(dv/dx)v2
  • Chain rule: dy/dx = (dy/du)·(du/dx) — differentiate the outer function, then multiply by the derivative of the inner function. Example: d/dx sin(x2) = cos(x2) · 2x.
  • Implicit differentiation: if x and y are mixed (e.g. x2 + y2 = a2), differentiate both sides w.r.t. x, treating y as a function of x (every y-term picks up a dy/dx).

entries.name: THEORY
entries.body:
THEORY:

Integration is the reverse process of differentiation — “which function, when differentiated, gives this?” That is why every indefinite integral carries a + C (constant of integration): all constants vanish on differentiation. The definite integral ∫ab f(x) dx gives the signed area under the curve between x = a and x = b.

entries.name: THEORY — Integration by Parts and Partial Fractions
entries.body:
THEORY — Integration by Parts and Partial Fractions:

By Parts: ∫ u·v dx = u ∫v dx − ∫ [ (du/dx) · ∫v dx ] dx.   Choose u by the ILATE order: Inverse trig → Logarithmic → Algebraic → Trigonometric → Exponential (whichever comes first becomes u).

Special pattern: ∫ ex [ f(x) + f′(x) ] dx = ex f(x) + C.

Partial fractions: for a proper rational function, split by denominator factors: 1(x − a)(x − b) = Ax − a + Bx − b ;   repeated factor (x − a)2 needs Ax − a + B(x − a)2 ;   an irreducible quadratic factor needs Ax + Bx2 + px + q. Then integrate term by term (every piece becomes a log or a tan−1).

entries.name: THEORY — Minors and Cofactors
entries.body:
THEORY — Minors and Cofactors:

The minor Mij of an element is the determinant left after deleting its row and column. The cofactor is Cij = (−1)i+j Mij — the sign follows a chessboard pattern starting with + at (1,1). The value of a determinant = sum of (elements of any row/column) × (their cofactors). The adjoint of A is the transpose of the cofactor matrix.

entries.name: PROPERTIES — Determinants (frequently asked)
entries.body:
PROPERTIES — Determinants (frequently asked):
  • Interchanging two rows (or columns) changes the sign of the determinant.
  • Two identical (or proportional) rows/columns → value = 0.
  • Multiplying one row by k multiplies the determinant by k; hence |kA| = kn|A| for an n×n matrix.
  • |AT| = |A|  |  |AB| = |A|·|B|  |  Determinant of a triangular/diagonal matrix = product of its diagonal entries.
  • Adding a multiple of one row to another row does not change the value (the key to simplifying determinants).
  • |A| = 0 ⇔ A is singular ⇔ A−1 does not exist. |A| ≠ 0 ⇔ non-singular ⇔ inverse exists.

entries.name: THEORY
entries.body:
THEORY:

The rank of a matrix is the number of independent rows (equivalently, the order of the largest non-zero minor). Method: apply elementary row operations to reach echelon form; the number of non-zero rows is the rank. Always rank ≤ min(number of rows, number of columns); the n×n identity matrix has rank n. Also rank(AB) ≤ min(rank A, rank B), and elementary operations never change the rank.

entries.section: System of Equations AX = B — All Methods and Rules
entries.name: THEORY — Consistency test (compare ranks)
entries.body:
THEORY — Consistency test (compare ranks):
  • rank(A) ≠ rank([A | B]) → no solution (inconsistent)
  • rank(A) = rank([A|B]) = number of unknowns n → unique solution
  • rank(A) = rank([A|B]) < n → infinitely many solutions
  • Homogeneous system AX = 0 is always consistent (x = 0 always works). A non-trivial solution exists ⇔ rank < n — for a square system, ⇔ |A| = 0.

Solution methods: (1) Matrix inversion: X = A−1B, valid only when |A| ≠ 0. (2) Cramer's rule (for |A| ≠ 0): x = DxD,   y = DyD,   z = DzD, where D is the coefficient determinant and Dx is D with the x-column replaced by the constants column (similarly for Dy, Dz). (3) Gauss elimination — echelon form of [A | B], then back substitution (works in all cases).

entries.name: THEORY
entries.body:
THEORY:

For a square matrix A, a scalar λ is an eigenvalue if there is a non-zero vector X with AX = λX — the matrix stretches X by λ without changing its direction; X is the eigenvector. Eigenvalues come from the characteristic equation |A − λI| = 0; for each λ, eigenvectors come from solving (A − λI)X = 0. Eigenvalues of AT are the same as those of A.

entries.name: THEORY — Cayley–Hamilton Theorem
entries.body:
THEORY — Cayley–Hamilton Theorem:

Every square matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation. Uses: (1) finding A−1 — write the characteristic equation, multiply by A−1, and rearrange; (2) expressing high powers (A3, A4, …) in terms of I and A (for 2×2) — which makes matrix-polynomial questions short.

THEORY:

The Taylor series rewrites a function as an infinite polynomial around a point x = a — this is how approximate values such as sin 31°, e0.1 or ln 1.02 are computed. The special case a = 0 is the Maclaurin series.

entries.name: RULE — How expansions are used in exams
entries.body:
RULE — How expansions are used in exams:

To expand a function “in powers of (x − a)”, either use the Taylor formula directly, or substitute t = x − a and use a standard Maclaurin expansion in t. To find an approximate value, keep only the first 2–3 terms — the later terms are negligibly small when |x| is small. sinh x = ex − e−x2, cosh x = ex + e−x2, and cosh2x − sinh2x = 1.

entries.name: Dⁿ [ eᵃˣ ]
entries.body: Dn [ eax ] = an eax    (D = d/dx)

entries.name: Dⁿ [ xⁿ ]
entries.body: Dn [ xn ] = n!

entries.name: Dⁿ [ sin(ax + b) ]
entries.body: Dn [ sin(ax + b) ] = an · sin(ax + b + nπ2)

entries.name: Dⁿ [ cos(ax + b) ]
entries.body: Dn [ cos(ax + b) ] = an · cos(ax + b + nπ2)

entries.name: Dⁿ [ (ax + b)m ]
entries.body: Dn [ (ax + b)m ] = m(m−1)(m−2)…(m−n+1) · an · (ax + b)m−n

entries.name: Dⁿ [ 1
entries.body: Dn [ 1x + a ] = (−1)n n!(x + a)n+1

entries.name: Dⁿ [ ln(ax + b) ]
entries.body: Dn [ ln(ax + b) ] = (−1)n−1 (n−1)! an(ax + b)n

entries.name: Dⁿ [ eᵃˣ sin(bx + c) ]
entries.body: Dn [ eax sin(bx + c) ] = (a2 + b2)n/2 · eax · sin(bx + c + nφ),   where φ = tan−1ba

entries.name: THEORY — Leibnitz's Theorem (n-th derivative of a product)
entries.body:
THEORY — Leibnitz's Theorem (n-th derivative of a product):

(uv)(n) = nC0 unv + nC1 un−1v1 + nC2 un−2v2 + … + nCn u vn

Working trick: choose as one factor a polynomial (x2, x3, …) — its derivatives become 0 after a few steps, so the series stops early and the answer stays short.

entries.name: THEORY — Homogeneous functions
entries.body:
THEORY — Homogeneous functions:

f(x, y) is homogeneous of degree n if f(tx, ty) = tn f(x, y). Quick test: in every term, the total power of x and y together is the same — e.g. x3 + x2y + xy2 + y3 is homogeneous of degree 3. Partial derivative ∂u∂x means: differentiate w.r.t. x treating y as a constant.

entries.name: Euler's Theorem
entries.body: Euler's Theorem: if u is homogeneous of degree n, then   x·∂u∂x + y·∂u∂y = n·u

entries.name: Second-order form
entries.body: Second-order form: x2∂2u∂x2 + 2xy∂2u∂x∂y + y2∂2u∂y2 = n(n−1)·u

entries.name: If F(u) is homogeneous of degree n
entries.body: If F(u) is homogeneous of degree n:   x·∂u∂x + y·∂u∂y = n · F(u)F′(u)   (used when u = sin−1(…), tan−1(…), ln(…) etc. — first identify F and n, the rest is routine)

entries.name: Total derivative
entries.body: Total derivative (z = f(x, y), with x, y functions of t):   dzdt = ∂z∂x·dxdt + ∂z∂y·dydt

entries.name: Total differential
entries.body: Total differential: dz = ∂z∂x dx + ∂z∂y dy

entries.name: Approximate error
entries.body: Approximate error: Δz ≈ ∂z∂x Δx + ∂z∂y Δy

entries.name: Implicit function f(x, y) = 0
entries.body: Implicit function f(x, y) = 0: dydx = − ∂f/∂x∂f/∂y

entries.name: Jacobian
entries.body:
Jacobian: J = ∂(u, v)∂(x, y) = ∂u∂x   ∂u∂y
∂v∂x   ∂v∂y    and   J · J′ = 1, where J′ = ∂(x, y)∂(u, v)

entries.name: THEORY
entries.body:
THEORY:

If J = 0, then u and v are functionally dependent — one can be expressed in terms of the other (e.g. u = x + y and v = (x + y)2). If J ≠ 0, they are independent. The chain rule for Jacobians also holds: ∂(u, v)∂(x, y) = ∂(u, v)∂(s, t) · ∂(s, t)∂(x, y).

entries.section: Maxima and Minima of f(x, y)
entries.name: THEORY — Method (steps)
entries.body:
THEORY — Method (steps):
  • Step 1: Solve ∂f∂x = 0 and ∂f∂y = 0 together to get the stationary points.
  • Step 2: At each point compute r = ∂2f∂x2,   s = ∂2f∂x∂y,   t = ∂2f∂y2.
  • Step 3: Decide by rt − s2: > 0 with r < 0 → Maximum । > 0 with r > 0 → Minimum । < 0 → Saddle point (neither max nor min) । = 0 → Doubtful case, needs further investigation.

entries.name: Definition
entries.body: Definition: Γ(n) = ∫0∞ e−x xn−1 dx   (n > 0)

entries.name: Γ( (1)/(2) )
entries.body: Γ(12) = √π

entries.name: For whole numbers
entries.body: For whole numbers: Γ(n + 1) = n!   (e.g. Γ(5) = 4! = 24)

entries.name: Useful values
entries.body: Useful values: Γ(32) = √π2

entries.name: Γ( (5)/(2) )
entries.body: Γ(52) = 3√π4

entries.name: Γ( (7)/(2) )
entries.body: Γ(72) = 15√π8   (each step multiplies by the previous n)

entries.name: Reflection formula
entries.body: Reflection formula: Γ(n) · Γ(1 − n) = πsin(nπ)

entries.name: Duplication formula
entries.body: Duplication formula: Γ(n) · Γ(n + 12) = √π22n−1 · Γ(2n)

entries.name: THEORY
entries.body:
THEORY:

The Gamma function is the extension of the factorial to fractions and all positive real numbers: Γ(n + 1) = n! is the bridge. Whenever an integral contains e−xxn−1 from 0 to ∞, or a product of Gamma values is asked, these relations are the entire method: reduce every argument step-by-step (using Γ(n+1) = nΓ(n)) until it reaches 1, 1/2, or a whole-number factorial.

entries.name: Definition
entries.body: Definition: B(m, n) = ∫01 xm−1 (1 − x)n−1 dx

entries.name: Infinite form
entries.body: Infinite form: B(m, n) = ∫0∞ xm−1(1 + x)m+n dx

entries.name: Beta–Gamma relation
entries.body: Beta–Gamma relation: B(m, n) = Γ(m) · Γ(n)Γ(m + n)

entries.name: Symmetry
entries.body: Symmetry: B(m, n) = B(n, m)

entries.name: Trigonometric form
entries.body: Trigonometric form: B(m, n) = 2 ∫0π/2 sin2m−1θ · cos2n−1θ dθ

entries.name: The famous shortcut that follows
entries.body: The famous shortcut that follows: ∫0π/2 sinmx · cosnx dx = Γ(m+12) · Γ(n+12)2 · Γ(m+n+22)

entries.section: Wallis' Formula and the Reduction Formula
entries.name: Reduction formula
entries.body: Reduction formula: if In = ∫0π/2 sinnx dx, then   In = n − 1n · In−2   (keep reducing until I0 = π/2 or I1 = 1)

entries.section: Wallis' Formula and the Reduction Formula
entries.name: Wallis — n even
entries.body: Wallis — n even: ∫0π/2 sinnx dx = (n−1)(n−3)…1n(n−2)…2 × π2

entries.section: Wallis' Formula and the Reduction Formula
entries.name: Wallis — n odd
entries.body: Wallis — n odd: ∫0π/2 sinnx dx = (n−1)(n−3)…2n(n−2)…3   (no π/2 factor)

entries.section: Wallis' Formula and the Reduction Formula
entries.name: Famous result
entries.body: Famous result: ∫0π/2 ln(sin x) dx = − π2 ln 2

entries.name: King's property
entries.body: King's property: ∫ab f(x) dx = ∫ab f(a + b − x) dx   — replacing x by (a + b − x) often makes a hard integral easy; adding the two forms is the standard trick

entries.name: ∫−aᵃ f(x) dx
entries.body: ∫−aa f(x) dx: = 2 ∫0a f(x) dx if f is even (f(−x) = f(x));   = 0 if f is odd (f(−x) = −f(x))

entries.name: ∫0²ᵃ f(x) dx
entries.body: ∫02a f(x) dx: = 2 ∫0a f(x) dx if f(2a − x) = f(x);   = 0 if f(2a − x) = −f(x)

entries.name: ∫0ᵃ f(x) dx
entries.body: ∫0a f(x) dx = ∫0a f(a − x) dx

entries.name: Swapping limits
entries.body: Swapping limits: ∫ab f = − ∫ba f

entries.name: ∫aᵃ f
entries.body: ∫<sub>a</sub><sup>a</sup> f = 0

entries.name: ∫aᵇ f
entries.body: ∫<sub>a</sub><sup>b</sup> f = ∫<sub>a</sub><sup>c</sup> f + ∫<sub>c</sub><sup>b</sup> f

entries.name: The a/2 shortcut
entries.body: The a/2 shortcut: ∫0a f(x)f(x) + f(a − x) dx = a2   — the answer without integrating at all

entries.name: THEORY
entries.body:
THEORY:

∬R f(x, y) dA is the volume under the surface z = f(x, y) over the region R. With f = 1 it gives the area of R. Evaluation is iterative: integrate with respect to one variable (holding the other constant), then the other. Change of order of integration means reversing this order — the method is always: (1) sketch the region from the given limits, (2) re-read the limits in the other direction using strips parallel to the other axis. There is no formula for the new limits — the sketch gives them.

entries.name: Area of region R
entries.body: Area of region R: A = ∬R dA = ∬R dy dx

entries.name: Volume under z = f(x, y)
entries.body: Volume under z = f(x, y): V = ∬R f(x, y) dA

entries.name: Area between two curves
entries.body: Area between two curves y = f(x) and y = g(x) (f above g), from a to b:   A = ∫ab [ f(x) − g(x) ] dx

entries.name: Polar transformation
entries.body: Polar transformation: x = r cosθ,   y = r sinθ,   dx dy → r dr dθ   (the extra factor r is the Jacobian — forgetting it is the most common error)

entries.name: THEORY
entries.body:
THEORY:

∭V f(x, y, z) dV extends the same idea to three dimensions; with f = 1 it gives the volume of the solid. Evaluate it as three nested single integrals, innermost first, using the surfaces that bound the solid as limits.

entries.name: Volume of a solid
entries.body: Volume of a solid: V = ∭ dV = ∭ dz dy dx (order as per the limits given)

entries.name: Spherical polar coordinates
entries.body: Spherical polar coordinates: x = r sinφ cosθ,   y = r sinφ sinθ,   z = r cosφ ;   dV = r2 sinφ dr dφ dθ   (best for spheres)

entries.name: Cylindrical polar coordinates
entries.body: Cylindrical polar coordinates: x = r cosθ,   y = r sinθ,   z = z ;   dV = r dr dθ dz   (best for cylinders)

entries.name: Area under a curve
entries.body: Area under a curve y = f(x), from a to b:   A = ∫ab y dx

entries.name: THEORY — Order, Degree, and the Shape of the Answer
entries.body:
THEORY — Order, Degree, and the Shape of the Answer:
  • Order = the order of the highest derivative present (y″ present → order 2).
  • Degree = the power of that highest derivative — defined only when the equation is a polynomial in the derivatives (no derivative inside a root or a fraction).
  • General solution = CF + PI. The CF (Complementary Function) is the solution of the homogeneous equation f(D)y = 0 and contains all the arbitrary constants (as many as the order). The PI (Particular Integral) is any one solution produced by the right-hand side Q(x).

entries.name: 1. Variable separable
entries.body: 1. Variable separable: dydx = f(x)·g(y) → rewrite as dyg(y) = f(x) dx and integrate both sides.

entries.name: 2. Homogeneous
entries.body: 2. Homogeneous: dydx = F(yx) → substitute y = v·x, so that dydx = v + xdvdx; the equation becomes separable in v and x. (Equations reducible to this form use the shift x = X + h, y = Y + k to remove constants.)

entries.name: 3. Exact equation
entries.body: 3. Exact equation: M dx + N dy = 0 is exact ⇔ ∂M∂y = ∂N∂x

entries.name: Solution of an exact equation
entries.body: Solution of an exact equation: ∫ M dx (treating y as constant) + ∫ (those terms of N which do not contain x) dy = C

entries.name: 4. Linear equation
entries.body: 4. Linear equation: dydx + P(x)·y = Q(x)

entries.name: THEORY — Linear equation, step by step
entries.body:
THEORY — Linear equation, step by step:
  • Step 1: First force the equation into the exact form above — the coefficient of dy/dx must be 1.
  • Step 2: Integrating Factor: IF = e∫ P dx.
  • Step 3: Write the solution directly: y · IF = ∫ (Q · IF) dx + C.
  • The same method works with roles swapped: dxdy + P1(y)·x = Q1(y) has IF = e∫ P1 dy and solution x · IF = ∫ (Q1 · IF) dy + C.

entries.name: 5. Bernoulli's equation
entries.body: 5. Bernoulli's equation: dydx + P·y = Q·yn → divide throughout by yn, then substitute z = y1−n; it becomes a linear equation in z — solve by the IF method.

entries.name: Auxiliary equation
entries.body: Auxiliary equation: in f(D)y = 0, replace D by m: f(m) = 0. Its roots decide the CF:

entries.name: CF — two distinct real roots m1, m2
entries.body: CF — two distinct real roots m1, m2: y = C1em1x + C2em2x

entries.name: CF — equal roots m, m
entries.body: CF — equal roots m, m: y = (C1 + C2x) emx   (for a triple root: (C1 + C2x + C3x2)emx — each repetition adds one more power of x)

entries.name: CF — complex roots α ± iβ
entries.body: CF — complex roots α ± iβ: y = eαx ( C1 cos βx + C2 sin βx )   (if the same pair repeats, multiply the bracket by (C3 + C4x) for the repeated pair)

entries.name: CF — purely imaginary roots ± iβ (α = 0)
entries.body: CF — purely imaginary roots ± iβ (α = 0): y = C1 cos βx + C2 sin βx

entries.name: Roots 0, 0
entries.body: Roots 0, 0: y = C1 + C2x

entries.section: Particular Integral (PI) — The Four Working Rules
entries.name: PI-1 · For eᵃˣ
entries.body: PI-1 · For eax: 1f(D) eax = eaxf(a)   (put D = a)

entries.section: Particular Integral (PI) — The Four Working Rules
entries.name: Failure case f(a)
entries.body: Failure case f(a) = 0:   = x · eaxf′(a)   (multiply by x and use f′(a); if that is also 0, repeat with x2/2! and f″(a))

entries.section: Particular Integral (PI) — The Four Working Rules
entries.name: PI-2 · For sin ax / cos ax
entries.body: PI-2 · For sin ax / cos ax: in a function of D2 only, replace D2 by −a2. If the denominator then becomes 0, multiply by x and differentiate the denominator w.r.t. D before substituting.

entries.section: Particular Integral (PI) — The Four Working Rules
entries.name: PI-3 · For xm (polynomial)
entries.body: PI-3 · For xm (polynomial): expand 1f(D) in ascending powers of D using the binomial series (keep only as many terms as needed — terms beyond Dm vanish on xm), then operate term by term.

entries.section: Particular Integral (PI) — The Four Working Rules
entries.name: PI-4 · For eᵃˣ·V(x) (Shift theorem)
entries.body: PI-4 · For eax·V(x) (Shift theorem): 1f(D) eax V = eax · 1f(D + a) V   (pull eax out; every D inside becomes D + a; then apply rules 1–3 to V)

entries.name: Form
entries.body: Form: x2y″ + a·x·y′ + b·y = 0   (recognition mark: the coefficient of each derivative carries exactly the matching power of x)

entries.name: Substitution
entries.body: Substitution: put x = ez; then   xD → θ,   x2D2 → θ(θ − 1),   where θ = ddz — the equation becomes a constant-coefficient equation in z, solved by the CF rules above; convert back with z = ln x at the end.

entries.name: Powers of i
entries.body: Powers of i: i2 = −1,   i3 = −i,   i4 = 1 — the cycle repeats every 4 (so i17 = i1 = i)

entries.name: z = x + iy
entries.body: z = x + iy: Re(z) = x,   Im(z) = y,   conjugate z̄ = x − iy

entries.name: Modulus
entries.body: Modulus: |z| = √(x2 + y2)

entries.name: z · z̄
entries.body: z · z̄ = |z|<sup>2</sup>

entries.name: |z1z2|
entries.body: |z<sub>1</sub>z<sub>2</sub>| = |z<sub>1</sub>|·|z<sub>2</sub>|

entries.name: | (z1)/(z2) |
entries.body: |z1z2| = |z1||z2|

entries.name: Triangle inequality
entries.body: Triangle inequality: |z1 + z2| ≤ |z1| + |z2|

entries.name: Argument
entries.body: Argument: arg z = tan−1yx — always correct it for the quadrant of the point (x, y); the principal value satisfies −π < arg z ≤ π

entries.name: Polar form
entries.body: Polar form: z = r(cos θ + i sin θ) = r·eiθ,   where r = |z| and θ = arg z

entries.name: Euler's formula
entries.body: Euler's formula: eiθ = cos θ + i sin θ

entries.name: De Moivre's theorem
entries.body: De Moivre's theorem: (cos θ + i sin θ)n = cos(nθ) + i sin(nθ)

entries.section: Analytic Functions and the Cauchy–Riemann Equations
entries.name: THEORY
entries.body:
THEORY:

f(z) = u + iv is analytic in a region if it is differentiable at every point of that region. The working test is the pair of Cauchy–Riemann (C–R) equations: analyticity ⇒ C–R hold (and where the partial derivatives are continuous, C–R holding is also sufficient). A further fact used constantly: the derivative of an analytic function is itself analytic.

entries.section: Analytic Functions and the Cauchy–Riemann Equations
entries.name: C–R equations (Cartesian)
entries.body: C–R equations (Cartesian): ∂u∂x = ∂v∂y    and    ∂u∂y = − ∂v∂x

entries.section: Analytic Functions and the Cauchy–Riemann Equations
entries.name: C–R equations (Polar)
entries.body: C–R equations (Polar): ∂u∂r = 1r∂v∂θ    and    ∂v∂r = − 1r∂u∂θ

entries.section: Analytic Functions and the Cauchy–Riemann Equations
entries.name: f′(z) from C–R
entries.body: f′(z) from C–R: f′(z) = ∂u∂x + i ∂v∂x = ∂u∂x − i ∂u∂y = ∂v∂y + i ∂v∂x

entries.name: THEORY
entries.body:
THEORY:

A function is harmonic if it satisfies Laplace's equation ∂2u∂x2 + ∂2u∂y2 = 0. If f = u + iv is analytic, both u and v are harmonic, and v is called the harmonic conjugate of u.

Finding the conjugate v from u: write dv = ∂v∂x dx + ∂v∂y dy, replace ∂v∂x by −∂u∂y and ∂v∂y by ∂u∂x (from C–R), then integrate: v = ∫ −∂u∂y dx + ∫ (terms of ∂u∂x free of x) dy + C.

Milne–Thomson method (constructing f(z) from u or v): compute ux and uy, then put x → z, y → 0 in them: f′(z) = ux(z, 0) − i·uy(z, 0). Integrate w.r.t. z to get f(z) (a real constant may remain undetermined). If u − v or u + v is given instead, first recover u using u = (u + v) + (u − v)2-type relations, then apply the same method.

entries.section: Complex Integration — Cauchy's Theorems and Formulas
entries.name: Line integral
entries.body: Line integral: ∫C f(z) dz — evaluated by parametrising the curve (e.g. z = z(t)) or by using the theorems below

entries.section: Complex Integration — Cauchy's Theorems and Formulas
entries.name: ML-inequality
entries.body: ML-inequality: | ∫C f(z) dz | ≤ M · L   (M = maximum of |f| on C, L = length of C)

entries.section: Complex Integration — Cauchy's Theorems and Formulas
entries.name: THEORY — Cauchy's Integral Theorem
entries.body:
THEORY — Cauchy's Integral Theorem:

If f(z) is analytic in a simply connected region, then around every closed curve C in that region, ∮C f(z) dz = 0. Consequence used in problems: the integral between two points is independent of the path, as long as the function stays analytic in between.

entries.section: Complex Integration — Cauchy's Theorems and Formulas
entries.name: ∮ dz
entries.body: ∮ dzz − a = 2πi   (if a lies inside C; if a is outside C, the value is 0)

entries.section: Complex Integration — Cauchy's Theorems and Formulas
entries.name: ∮ dz (2)
entries.body: ∮ dz(z − a)n = 0   (for every integer n ≥ 2, even when a is inside C)

entries.section: Complex Integration — Cauchy's Theorems and Formulas
entries.name: Cauchy's Integral Formula
entries.body: Cauchy's Integral Formula: f(a) = 12πi ∮ f(z)z − a dz   — the value at one interior point is fixed by the values on the boundary

entries.section: Complex Integration — Cauchy's Theorems and Formulas
entries.name: Cauchy's Formula for derivatives
entries.body: Cauchy's Formula for derivatives: f(n)(a) = n!2πi ∮ f(z)(z − a)n+1 dz

entries.section: Complex Integration — Cauchy's Theorems and Formulas
entries.name: RULE — How Unit V problems are solved
entries.body:
RULE — How Unit V problems are solved:

(1) Factor the denominator and find which singular points lie inside the given curve (|z − a| < radius tests). (2) Points outside contribute 0. (3) For each inside point, split by partial fractions into terms of the form f(z)(z − a)n+1 and apply Cauchy's formula (n = 0) or the derivative formula (n ≥ 1). (4) Add the contributions and multiply out the 2πi factors carefully — most errors in this unit are sign and 2πi errors, not concept errors.
